slides.title: The analyst's two main tools
points: Spreadsheets handle quick models and small data; SQL pulls and summarises large data from databases.
Most business analysis uses both.

slides.title: Clean structure, traceable logic
points: Keep raw data, calculations and outputs on separate sheets.
Use lookups (XLOOKUP), pivot tables and named ranges instead of hard-typed numbers.
In SQL: filter, join, group and aggregate before exporting, so the spreadsheet stays small.
Every number should be traceable back to its source.

slides.title: Quick against reliable
points: Spreadsheets are fast to build and easy to break silently (a pasted value over a formula).
Large data in spreadsheets gets slow and error-prone; query it instead.
Shared spreadsheets without version control drift.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A data tab refreshed from a saved query.
Checks: totals that must match the source.
Colour conventions: inputs one colour, formulas another.

slides.title: Numbers that describe a business's future
points: A financial model projects revenue, costs and cash from assumptions, to support a decision: a price, a hire, an investment.
Its value is in clear assumptions and scenarios.

slides.title: Drivers, statements, scenarios
points: Start from drivers (customers, price, churn, cost per unit), not from last year's totals plus a percentage.
Link the three statements: income statement, balance sheet, cash flow.
Build scenarios (base, downside, upside) and sensitivity tables for key assumptions.
Cash matters more than profit for survival.

slides.title: Detail against usefulness
points: Too much detail hides the few assumptions that matter.
Precise-looking outputs from guessed inputs mislead.
Models need owners and dated versions.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: An assumptions sheet up front.
Sensitivity tables showing which input moves the result most.
Monthly comparison of actuals with the model.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: The few numbers that track what matters
points: Key performance indicators (KPIs) measure progress toward a goal: revenue growth, retention, cost per acquisition.
Good KPIs drive decisions; bad ones drive gaming.

slides.title: Leading and lagging
points: Lagging indicators show results (revenue); leading indicators predict them (qualified pipeline).
Each KPI has a precise definition, a source, an owner and a target.
Pair a KPI with a counter-metric to prevent gaming (speed with quality).
Few KPIs per team; if everything is key, nothing is.

slides.title: What gets measured gets managed
points: A target can distort behaviour (closing tickets fast but badly).
Vanity metrics (page views) look good and drive nothing.
Definitions change; record when and why.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A one-page dashboard per team.
Weekly reviews of trends, not single points.
Definitions documented in a shared glossary.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Turning analysis into a decision
points: Analysis is only useful if decision-makers understand it and act.
Presenting well means leading with the answer.

slides.title: Answer, evidence, ask
points: Start with the conclusion and the recommendation.
Support it with two or three pieces of evidence, each with one clear chart.
State assumptions and risks plainly.
End with the decision or action you need.

slides.title: Simple without misleading
points: Too much detail loses the audience; too little loses credibility. Keep an appendix.
Charts with truncated axes exaggerate; keep them honest.
Tailor depth to the audience.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: One-page memos before meetings.
Chart titles that state the takeaway.
A clear owner and date for the next step.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Finding the right problem before building
points: Discovery works out what problem is worth solving and whether a solution will work, before committing to build it.
It reduces the risk of building something nobody needs.

slides.title: Talk, test, learn
points: Interview users about their real behaviour and problems, not their opinions of your idea.
Frame opportunities from evidence; generate several solutions.
Test the riskiest assumption cheaply first: a prototype, a fake door, a concierge test.
Decide with evidence: build, change or drop.

slides.title: Learning against shipping
points: Too little discovery builds the wrong thing; too much never ships.
Users can't always say what they want; watch what they do.
Confirmation bias: seek evidence that could prove you wrong.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Weekly customer conversations by the product trio (product, design, engineering).
Assumption maps and experiment logs.
Prototypes tested before specs are written.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Choosing what to do first
points: There's always more to do than capacity allows. Prioritisation decides what goes first, and what doesn't happen.
Saying no is most of it.

slides.title: Value, effort, confidence
points: Tie priorities to goals: what moves the outcome the team owns?
Frameworks like RICE (reach, impact, confidence, effort) make reasoning comparable.
Consider risk and dependencies, not just value.
Revisit priorities as evidence changes.

slides.title: Frameworks help, judgement decides
points: Scores can give false precision; use them to discuss, not to decide alone.
The loudest stakeholder isn't the most important customer.
Too many top priorities means none.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A ranked list, not tiers of 'high'.
Clear 'not now' decisions communicated with reasons.
Quarterly reprioritisation against goals.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Measuring whether the product works for people
points: Product metrics track how people find, use and stay with a product: activation, engagement, retention, conversion.
They show whether changes actually help.

slides.title: A north star and its inputs
points: A north-star metric captures the value users get (for example, weekly active teams collaborating).
Input metrics are the levers that drive it (sign-ups activated, features adopted).
Funnels show where people drop off; cohorts show whether they stay.
Experiments prove whether a change moved the metric.

slides.title: Measuring what matters
points: Easy-to-measure metrics (clicks) can mislead about value.
Short-term gains can hurt long-term retention.
Too many metrics dilute focus.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A metrics tree from the north star to team-level inputs.
Retention curves by cohort.
Every launch with a success metric defined in advance.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Communicating direction over time
points: A roadmap shows what a team plans to work on and why, over the coming months.
Good roadmaps communicate outcomes and priorities, not fixed promises.

slides.title: Now, next, later
points: Organise by problems or outcomes rather than feature lists.
Use time horizons: now (committed), next (likely), later (exploring).
Tie each item to a goal, so trade-offs are visible.
Update regularly and share what changed.

slides.title: Clarity against flexibility
points: Date-heavy roadmaps become broken promises.
Vague roadmaps leave sales and partners unable to plan.
Different audiences need different detail.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A public roadmap with themes, an internal one with detail.
Quarterly reviews of what shipped and what moved.
Clear language about confidence levels.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Getting a product into people's hands well
points: A launch coordinates engineering, marketing, sales, support and operations so a release reaches the right people and works.
Many good features fail through poor launches.

slides.title: Ready, gradual, measured
points: Readiness: documentation, support training, sales materials, monitoring.
Release gradually (beta, percentage rollout) where possible.
Define success metrics and watch them from day one.
Have a rollback plan and an owner for launch day.

slides.title: Big splash against safe rollout
points: A big-bang launch gets attention and concentrates risk.
Launching too quietly means nobody finds the feature.
Delaying for perfection loses momentum and learning.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A launch checklist and go/no-go meeting.
Internal dogfooding before public release.
A post-launch review at two to four weeks.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Understanding people before designing for them
points: Design research studies users' needs, behaviours and contexts so designs solve real problems.
It ranges from interviews to usability tests to analytics.

slides.title: Methods for questions
points: Generative research (interviews, field studies) explores needs.
Evaluative research (usability tests) checks whether a design works.
Five users in a usability test reveal most major problems.
Synthesise findings into insights the team can act on.

slides.title: Rigour against speed
points: Small studies are fast and directional, not statistically conclusive.
Recruiting the wrong participants gives misleading answers.
Research that isn't shared changes nothing.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: Research plans with clear questions.
Recorded sessions and highlight reels for the team.
Insight repositories.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: How people and products talk to each other
points: Interaction design shapes how a product responds to people: flows, controls, feedback and states.
Good interaction design feels obvious.

slides.title: Clarity, feedback, forgiveness
points: Make the next action clear; one primary action per screen.
Give immediate feedback for every action (pressed, loading, done, failed).
Design every state: empty, loading, error, partial, success.
Let people undo and recover from mistakes.

slides.title: Simple against powerful
points: More options give power and add confusion.
Novel interactions can delight and confuse; familiar patterns are learned already.
Hiding things declutters and can make them undiscoverable.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: User flows and wireframes before visual design.
Prototypes tested with users.
Design system components for consistent behaviour.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Consistent look across a product
points: A visual system defines type, colour, spacing, icons and components so every screen looks and feels like one product.
It speeds design and building, and improves accessibility.

slides.title: Tokens, scale, components
points: Design tokens name values (colours, spacing, type sizes) used everywhere.
A type scale and spacing scale give rhythm and hierarchy.
Colour with purpose and sufficient contrast; never colour alone to convey meaning.
Reusable components with documented usage.

slides.title: Consistency against expression
points: A rigid system can feel bland; a loose one fragments.
Systems need maintenance and ownership.
Adoption matters more than completeness.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A shared component library in design tools and code.
Light and dark themes from the same tokens.
Contribution guidelines for new components.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

slides.title: Showing how you think, not just what you made
points: A design portfolio is the main evidence hiring teams use to judge a designer.
They want to see process and impact, not only polished screens.

slides.title: Case studies that tell a story
points: Three or four strong case studies beat many thin ones.
Each: the problem, your role, the process (research, options, trade-offs), the result.
Show decisions and what you learned, including what didn't work.
Quantify impact where you can.

slides.title: Depth against skimmability
points: Reviewers skim; lead each case with a short summary.
Confidential work needs anonymising; never share what you can't.
Concept projects are fine if framed honestly.

slides.title: What you'll see at work
points: A portfolio walkthrough round in interviews.
A one-page summary per case study.
Updated after each significant project.

slides.title: One question
points: Answer it, then read the why.

newQuestions.stem: A forecast spreadsheet has numbers typed directly into formulas, like =B4*1.07. What's the problem?
choices: The 7 % assumption is hidden and can't be changed in one place; put it in a labelled input cell and reference it
why: Hard-coded assumptions are hard to find, check and update.

newQuestions.stem: A model shows a profitable year, but the company runs out of cash in month 7. How?
choices: Profit isn't cash: customers pay late, inventory and upfront costs use cash before revenue arrives; model cash flow
why: Timing of cash in and out can sink a profitable business.
Possible, but the pattern is a classic cash-timing gap.

newQuestions.stem: A support team's KPI is 'tickets closed per day'. Closures rise, and customer satisfaction falls. What's missing?
choices: A counter-metric such as reopened tickets or satisfaction, so speed doesn't replace quality
why: Pairing metrics stops one being gamed at the expense of the goal.

newQuestions.stem: You have five minutes with an executive. How should you open?
choices: With the recommendation and the one number that supports it
With a history of the project
With a table of all the data
why: Executives decide on the answer first, then probe.

newQuestions.stem: In user interviews, which question gives more reliable evidence?
choices: 'Tell me about the last time you did this. What happened?'
'Would you use a feature that does X?'
'How much would you pay for it in the future?'
why: Past behaviour reveals real needs; hypothetical answers are unreliable.
Future intent is a poor predictor.

newQuestions.stem: Every item on the backlog is labelled 'P1'. What's the fix?
choices: Force-rank the items against the goal, so there's one order and an explicit cut line
Work on all of them at once
why: A single ranked order makes trade-offs explicit.

newQuestions.stem: A redesign increases clicks on the home page by 30 %, but monthly retention drops. Was it a success?
choices: Probably not: retention reflects lasting value; investigate why people engage more but stay less
Clicks and retention are the same
why: The north-star outcome got worse; clicks may show confusion.

newQuestions.stem: Sales keeps promising customers features from the 'later' column with specific dates. What would help?
choices: Make confidence explicit (committed / likely / exploring), keep dates only on committed work, and align with sales on what can be promised
why: Clear confidence levels prevent false promises.

newQuestions.stem: On launch day, support is flooded with questions they can't answer about the new feature. What was missed?
choices: Readiness: support should have been trained and given docs before launch
why: Launch readiness includes the people who answer customers.

newQuestions.stem: You want to know whether people can complete checkout in the new design. Which method fits best?
choices: A usability test: watch representative users try the task and note where they struggle
A survey asking if they like the colours
why: Observing real attempts shows whether the design works.

newQuestions.stem: A form shows no response after 'Submit' while the server works for three seconds, so users click again and submit twice. What's missing?
choices: Immediate feedback: a loading state and a disabled button while it submits
why: Feedback tells users their action registered and prevents repeats.

newQuestions.stem: Error states are shown only by turning text red. What's the accessibility problem and fix?
choices: Colour alone isn't perceivable by everyone; add an icon and a text message
why: People with colour vision deficiencies may miss it; text and icons don't rely on colour.

newQuestions.stem: Which portfolio case study is strongest?
choices: One that states the problem, your role, the options you considered, why you chose one, and the measured result
A gallery of final screens with no text
Twenty small projects with one image each
